headline: Appointed two senior planners, Jacob Alderman and Nicholas Corbo, as administrative officers; zoning, subdivision, and comprehensive plan workshops took no votes.
summary: Staff gave status updates on the zoning ordinance, subdivision regulations, and comprehensive plan. No votes were taken on those items. The commission voted unanimously to appoint two senior planners as administrative officers.
decisions: Appointed Jacob Alderman and Nicholas "Nico" Corbo as Administrative Officers, unanimously.

decision_evidence.quote: Motion to appoint Jacob Alderman and Nicholas "Nico" Corbo as Administrative Officers was made by Commissioner Kolodziej and seconded by Commissioner Esckilsen. The motion carried unanimously.

Pawtucket Planning Commission 
Pawtucket Municipal Annex Council Chambers (Second Floor) 
100 Freight Street 
Pawtucket, RI 02860   
 
Meeting Minutes 
Tuesday, September 15, 2026 
 
A. Opening/Call to Order  
Chairwoman Kolodziej called the Pawtucket Planning Commission meeting to order at 5:58 PM. 
 
B. Roll Call 
The following Planning Commission members were:  
 
Present (8): Chairwoman Karen Kolodziej, Monique Renaud, Lee Esckilsen, Christopher Fontes, Elizabeth 
Crowley, Jonas Bruggemann, Annmarie DeBrito, and Fabiola Alikpokou. 
 
Absent: (1): Vice-Chair Albert Vitali Jr 
 
Staff (3): Director Jason Pezzullo; Nicholas Corbo, Senior Planner; and Jacob Alderman, Senior Planner.  
 
C. General Public Comment 
No public comment 
 
D. Old Business 
Staff reported no items of old business.  
 
E. New Businesses 
Welcome New Staff Planners  
a. Jacob Alderman – Senior Planner 
b. Nicholas "Nico" Corbo – Senior Planner 
The Planning Director introduced the two new Senior Planners, Jacob Alderman and Nicholas "Nico" 
Corbo, both of whom recently relocated to the Federal Hill neighborhood of Providence. Jacob Alderman 
holds a Master's degree from the University of Florida and joined the department from Florida. Nicholas 
Corbo holds a Master's degree from Tufts University and relocated from Cambridge, Massachusetts. The 
Director noted that both planners are filling positions vacated by the departure of prior staff members 
Grace and Curtis, and that they have been performing well since joining the office.
All Planning Commission meetings are open meetings unless otherwise stated. The meeting location is accessible to people

8239 (TDD) not less than two (2) business days in advance of the hearing date. 
 
 
Appointment of Administrative Officers  
a. Jacob Alderman 
b. Nicholas "Nico" Corbo 
The Commission voted to appoint Jacob Alderman and Nicholas "Nico" Corbo as Administrative 
Officers, authorizing them to prepare and sign documents on behalf of the Commission. 
Motion to appoint Jacob Alderman and Nicholas "Nico" Corbo as Administrative Officers was made by 
Commissioner Kolodziej and seconded by Commissioner Esckilsen. The motion carried unanimously. 
Workshop — Text Amendments to the Zoning Ordinance (No Vote Taken) 
Senior Planner Nicholas Corbo presented a status update on the ongoing Zoning Ordinance update. He 
explained that the department intends to build upon the substantial draft work already completed by 
former staff, rather than start from scratch. The update is driven by several goals: ensuring alignment 
with 2026 Rhode Island legislative changes, improving the accessibility and plain-English readability of 
the ordinance for public-facing applicants, standardizing formatting and tables throughout, and making 
clerical corrections. Corbo noted that the city serves a multilingual population and that readability and 
translation considerations are a priority. 
The Planning Director added context regarding prior work on the ordinance, noting that several 
workshops had already been held with the Commission and multiple draft amendment packages had been 
developed. However, those prior drafts were never transmitted to City Council. Staff indicated that 
legislative updates from both the 2025 and 2026 sessions will be incorporated together into the new draft. 
The Director commented that the pace of state legislative change has made it increasingly difficult for 
municipalities to keep pace, and expressed the view that a period of stability in state zoning law would 
benefit all parties. 
Identified next steps include an in-depth staff review of prior zoning ordinance drafts, a review of 2024–
2026 legislative changes, case studies of recently updated zoning ordinances from surrounding 
municipalities, and the development of a project timeline with new draft documents to follow. 
Workshop — Text Amendments to the Land Development and Subdivision Regulations (No Vote 
Taken) 
Senior Planner Corbo continued with a parallel status update on the Land Development and Subdivision 
Regulations update. He noted that unlike the zoning ordinance, no formal workshops had yet been held 
on the subdivision regulations, and that the prior staff's work was in the drafting phase. The goals for this 
update mirror those for the zoning ordinance: plain-English language, improved applicant-facing 
checklists, grammatical and clerical corrections, and alignment with recent state legislative changes. 
A notable emphasis was placed on formalizing the pre-application meeting process. Staff noted that a 
recurring issue has been applicants submitting materials without prior contact, leaving staff without 
context and resulting in prolonged follow-up. The department intends to streamline this through more 
structured pre-application meetings, whether in-person or through an online portal. 
The discussion briefly touched on the state-mandated OpenGov platform, which is required for the 
submission of all subdivision and major land development applications. The Planning Director 
characterized the platform as a "solution looking for a problem," noting that many municipalities are 
struggling with its complexity and have not yet fully adopted it. Commissioner Bruggemann – who

works at the City of Cranston - confirmed that adoption had been difficult. Bruggemann described the 
setup process as "ham-fisted" and noted ongoing conversations with peer communities about best 
practices. The Director indicated that Pawtucket is currently using OpenGov for building permits and 
zoning applications, but is proceeding cautiously on the subdivision side until implementation challenges 
at the state level are resolved. 
Next steps include in-depth staff review of prior subdivision and land development regulation drafts, 
review of relevant legislative changes, and development of a project timeline. 
Workshop — Comprehensive Plan Update (No Vote Taken) 
Senior Planner Jacob Alderman presented an overview of the Comprehensive Plan update process. He 
noted that the City of Pawtucket's current Comprehensive Plan was last adopted in June 2017, and that 
Rhode Island state law mandates an update every ten years, bringing the city to the point of needing to 
initiate this process now. 
Alderman provided background on what a Comprehensive Plan entails: a community-centered document 
containing future goals and aligned policies across ten state-required topic areas, including land use, 
housing, economic development, historic resources, natural resources, recreation and open space, 
community services, transportation, implementation, and natural hazards. He noted that the existing 2017 
plan incorporates natural hazards within the natural resources chapter, but the state now requires it to be a 
standalone element. The plan must also look forward through a 20-year planning horizon—through 
approximately 2050—and include data collection and forecasting across all topic areas. 
Alderman outlined four general phases for the update: (1) data analysis and mapping, (2) community 
engagement, (3) drafting of goals and policies, and (4) formal adoption and state submission. He 
emphasized that phases one and two will proceed concurrently, and that the Commission will be closely 
involved throughout. On community engagement, he described a range of approaches, from early 
"visioning" sessions that solicit high-level community input before any drafting begins, to presenting 
draft chapters to the public for comment. He cited an example from a prior position in which 
municipalities posted draft plan content online and allowed public track-changes commentary. 
The Planning Director stressed that the plan will be developed entirely in-house, as no funding has been 
appropriated for a consultant. He noted that an application for a Community Readiness Grant through the 
Rhode Island Department of Commerce was submitted the prior year but was unsuccessful, and that 
additional funding requests would need to go through the next budget cycle. He estimated a timeline of 
18 to 24 months for a staff-produced plan, acknowledging the significant workload given competing 
priorities. 
Commission members engaged substantively in the discussion. Commissioner Esckilsen asked who 
drives the vision for the Comprehensive Plan, and the Director confirmed that the Planning Commission 
is effectively the author of the plan, with city council and the administration playing subsequent roles. 
Due to her prior experience drafting comprehensive plans for other communities, Commissioner 
Alikpokou strongly recommended pursuing budget appropriations for outside consultant support, at 
minimum for the community engagement and key chapters, characterizing the plan as "the bible of the 
community" and underscoring the significance of Pawtucket's ongoing growth and development activity. 
Commissioner Crowley suggested that the Commission draft and send a letter to the incoming mayor-
elect following inauguration, outlining the importance of the Comprehensive Plan and formally 
requesting the necessary resources. The Planning Director expressed support for this approach and 
offered to assist in drafting the advocacy letter when the time comes.

The group also briefly discussed the possibility of forming a subcommittee of the Planning Commission 
to assist with drafting plan chapters as they mature. The Director noted that community engagement 
efforts should be conducted at a neighborhood level across the city—through ward-based meetings and 
gatherings at community spaces—rather than in a single centralized forum, in order to maximize 
participation. 
F. Director's Report (No Vote Taken)  
The Planning Director provided an update on several active and anticipated development projects: 
The Gateway District is expected to see a major land development and subdivision application come 
before the Commission in the new year. 
The Tidewater development is progressing well. Approximately two-thirds of the project has already 
received Planning Commission approval. Infrastructure financing work, including bonding and 
borrowing agreements, was advancing, with a pre-project review agreement signing having taken place 
that morning. The pedestrian bridge and riverwalk components have secured full funding and are moving 
forward. 
The cities of Pawtucket and Central Falls jointly received a grant to acquire the Conant Thread property, 
a roughly 20-acre mill complex north of the station that straddles the municipal boundary between the 
two cities. The site was substantially damaged by fire. The grant will support site cleanup and 
preparation for future development. The Director noted that the state has projected up to 1,000 units of 
development potential on the site, characterizing the acquisition as "very ambitious" and significant for 
the region. 
Commissioner Crowley offered remarks recognizing the outgoing mayor for his sixteen years of tenure 
and the progress made during that time, including the reopening of the Conant Street Bridge after 35 
years of closure, work on the train station, and the conversion of vacant mill buildings. The 
Commissioner also acknowledged efforts that did not come to fruition, including work to preserve 
Memorial Hospital and the Pawtucket Red Sox stadium project, and expressed well wishes for the 
incoming administration. 
G. Adjournment  
Motion to adjourn was made and seconded. The motion carried unanimously.
